questions.stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that

options.text: the two alleles of a gene separate during the formation of gametes
dominant alleles are always more common than recessive alleles
all offspring resemble the dominant parent
alleles of different genes are always inherited together

questions.explanation: Because homologous chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles during meiosis I, the two alleles at any locus end up in different gametes. Each gamete therefore carries only one allele of each gene, which is why a Tt parent produces T and t gametes in equal numbers.

distractorRationale.b: Dominance describes how an allele is expressed, not how common it is in a population
distractorRationale.c: A heterozygous cross produces some offspring with the recessive phenotype
distractorRationale.d: Independent assortment says the opposite for genes on different chromosomes

questions.stem: A homozygous tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a homozygous dwarf plant (tt). What are the offspring?
questions.explanation: Every gamete from the TT parent carries T and every gamete from the tt parent carries t, so all offspring are Tt. Since T is dominant they all look tall, but each carries a hidden recessive allele.

distractorRationale.a: The recessive allele is masked by the dominant T in every offspring
distractorRationale.c: A 1 : 1 ratio results from Tt crossed with tt, not from TT crossed with tt
distractorRationale.d: A 3 : 1 ratio results from crossing two heterozygotes

questions.stem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants are crossed (Tt × Tt). What phenotypic ratio is expected among the offspring?
questions.explanation: Each parent produces T and t gametes equally, so the four possible combinations are TT, Tt, Tt and tt. Three of these contain at least one dominant T and are therefore tall, giving the classic 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio, while the underlying genotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.

distractorRationale.a: A 1 : 1 ratio comes from a test cross, Tt × tt
distractorRationale.c: One quarter of the offspring inherit t from both parents and are dwarf
distractorRationale.d: An intermediate phenotype would require incomplete dominance, which does not apply to pea height

questions.stem: A farmer has a tall pea plant but does not know whether it is TT or Tt. Which cross would settle the question, and how?

options.text: Cross it with a TT plant; dwarf offspring would show it is Tt
Cross it with a dwarf (tt) plant; any dwarf offspring would show it is Tt
Cross it with another tall plant of unknown genotype; the ratio will always be 3 : 1
Examine the plant's leaves under a microscope

questions.explanation: In a test cross the tt partner contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring reveal what the unknown parent contributed. If it is TT every offspring is Tt and tall; if it is Tt then half receive t from both parents and are dwarf, so even one dwarf offspring proves it is heterozygous.

distractorRationale.a: A TT partner masks everything, since every offspring inherits at least one T and is tall
distractorRationale.c: The ratio depends on both parents' genotypes, so an unknown partner gives an ambiguous result
distractorRationale.d: Genotype cannot be read from leaf appearance under a microscope

questions.stem: In a certain plant, red flower colour (R) is dominant to white (r). A cross between a heterozygous red plant and a white plant produces 60 offspring. Approximately how many are expected to be white?
questions.explanation: The cross is Rr × rr, which gives offspring in the ratio 1 Rr : 1 rr, so half are expected to be white. Half of 60 is 30. Note that this test cross gives a 1 : 1 ratio rather than the 3 : 1 of a heterozygous self-cross.

distractorRationale.a: 15 would be a quarter, which is the white proportion in an Rr × Rr cross
distractorRationale.b: 20 would be a third, which no monohybrid cross produces
distractorRationale.d: 45 is three quarters, the proportion that would be red in an Rr × Rr cross

questions.stem: In the four o'clock plant, a red-flowered plant crossed with a white-flowered plant gives all pink offspring, and crossing two pink plants gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. This pattern is called
questions.explanation: Under incomplete dominance neither allele fully masks the other, so the heterozygote has its own intermediate phenotype. Because all three genotypes now look different, the phenotypic ratio matches the genotypic ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 instead of collapsing to 3 : 1.

distractorRationale.a: Complete dominance would make the heterozygote indistinguishable from the dominant homozygote, giving 3 : 1
distractorRationale.c: Sex linkage concerns genes on the sex chromosomes and gives different results in males and females
distractorRationale.d: Independent assortment concerns the inheritance of two or more different genes

questions.stem: Two dwarf pea plants (tt) are crossed. What proportion of the offspring will be tall?
questions.explanation: Neither parent carries the dominant T allele, so no gamete can supply one and every offspring must be tt. A recessive characteristic breeds true, which is why homozygous recessive lines are so useful in test crosses.

distractorRationale.b: A quarter would require both parents to carry a hidden T allele
distractorRationale.c: A half would require one parent to be heterozygous
distractorRationale.d: Three quarters is the tall proportion in a Tt × Tt cross

questions.stem: If a cross predicts a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio, then in any family of four offspring exactly three must show the dominant characteristic.
questions.explanation: False. A 3 : 1 ratio expresses the probability for each individual offspring, three chances in four. Just as four coin tosses can all give heads, all four offspring could show the dominant characteristic; the ratio is only approached reliably in large numbers, which is why Mendel counted thousands of plants.

questions.stem: Two pea plants, both tall, are crossed and among their offspring a dwarf plant appears. What must the genotypes of the two parents have been?
questions.explanation: A dwarf plant is tt, so it received a recessive t allele from each parent, meaning both parents must carry t. Since both parents are tall they must each also carry T, so both were heterozygous Tt.

distractorRationale.a: Neither parent would carry a t allele, so no dwarf offspring could arise
distractorRationale.b: Only one parent could contribute t, and the other would always contribute T, so all offspring would be tall
distractorRationale.d: A tt parent would be dwarf, but the question states both parents were tall

questions.stem: In guinea pigs, black coat colour (B) is dominant to white (b). Using a Punnett square, work out the genotypic and phenotypic ratios expected when two heterozygous black guinea pigs are crossed. State Mendel's law that explains why each parent produces two kinds of gamete.
markingGuide: Symbols defined: B is the allele for black, b the allele for white, B dominant to b (1 mark)
Parental genotypes correctly stated as Bb and Bb, both black in phenotype (2 marks)
Gametes correctly shown: each parent produces B and b in equal proportion (2 marks)
Punnett square drawn and correctly filled with BB, Bb, Bb and bb (3 marks)
Genotypic ratio stated as 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb (1 mark)
Phenotypic ratio stated as 3 black : 1 white (1 mark)
Law of segregation stated: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation so that each gamete carries only one of them (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The cross gives a genotypic ratio of 1 : 2 : 1 and a phenotypic ratio of 3 black : 1 white, because BB and Bb both appear black while only bb is white. The law of segregation is what guarantees the two kinds of gamete, since the homologous chromosomes carrying B and b are separated in meiosis I.
